title.value: Quantifying Fold Geometry With GPS and Geostatistics

note.value:
With the advent of modern surveying techniques, including the use of differential GPS and DEM’s, we are able to quantify the geometry of geologic structures with spatially-extensive, high-resolution, high-density data sets. These data alone can provide many insights into the formation of structures; however, by combining these data with geostatistical tools we can create regularly gridded three-dimensional structural models that provide additional insights into structural geometry and underlying physical processes. These efforts parallel in many ways the approach taken in industry to map stratigraphic horizons from seismic data and/or well picks.

In the Western Grand Canyon we have collected more than 24,000 GPS point locations over a ~30 square km area in order to map out deformation associated with a normal fault system (see this volume, contribution F, Figure 3). These points have horizontal measurement errors of ~ 1 m and vertical errors of ~ 3 m. Additional errors from a marker horizon are associated with erosion of surfaces and stratigraphic variations. Total vertical errors are thus on the order of ±5 m. The data are highly clustered spatially due to the limited extent of outcrops, so although a series of cross-sections can reasonably be constructed by extrapolation, the determination of along strike continuity is more difficult.

We are in the process of creating a 3-dimensional structure contour grid from the GPS survey data using ordinary Kriging with locally-varying second-order trend. This approach allows for inclusion of both the large-scale structure as a second-order polynomial fit (Fig. 1) and local variation from this polynomial through analysis of the local variance (Fig. 2). Ordinary kriging is a linear estimation procedure that attempts to minimize both the variance of the estimation errors and generate a mean residual error near zero (Isaaks and Srivastava, 1989). Kriging accounts for the data variance and data redundancy when estimating a grid point. It is also possible to include asymmetry in the variance analysis so , for example, data along strike can be given more weight in estimating a value than data in a dip direction. Inclusion of a “nugget effect”, variance associated with data collected from the same location, can account for measurement noise in the data.

The resulting gridded surface (Fig 3) allows both visual and quantitative analysis of the structures associated with a continental normal fault system. We plan to use the surface as a tool for analyzing structural variation along strike associated with changes in fault slip and fault geometry.
Resor, Phil. (2003). Quantifying Fold Geometry With GPS and Geostatistics. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/wx030yc1223
